messages.message: What problem does the Transformer solve that RNN-based sequence-to-sequence models could not?

The paper argues that recurrent models compute hidden states h_t from h_{t-1} and the input at position t, which inherently prevents parallelisation within a training example (§1). At long sequence lengths this also constrains batch size because of memory. The Transformer replaces recurrence with attention, so all positions are computed in parallel, cutting training time and improving quality on WMT 2014 EN-DE and EN-FR (Table 2).
Why is sequential processing a bottleneck for training on GPUs?

Sequential state means step t must finish before step t+1 can start, which serialises the forward pass along the time axis. Modern accelerators want big parallel matmuls; a serial chain of small ops leaves them underutilised. The Transformer sidesteps this by making every position's representation depend on every other position through one attention matmul that GPUs execute in parallel (§1).
What role did attention play in seq2seq models before this paper?

Attention was added on top of an RNN encoder-decoder to let the decoder look at any encoder position instead of squeezing everything through the final encoder hidden state. The paper cites Bahdanau et al. 2015 for that use of attention. What was novel here was making attention the *only* mechanism — no recurrence, no convolutions (§2).
What is the path length problem in learning long-range dependencies?

In an RNN, gradient signal between positions i and j must flow through |i − j| recurrent steps, so it decays or explodes with distance. In a CNN like ConvS2S it flows through O(log_k(n)) layers where k is the kernel width. In self-attention it's a constant one hop, so gradients see arbitrary-distance dependencies in one step (§4, Table 1).
What were the prior architectures the paper explicitly compared itself against?

The paper compares against the Extended Neural GPU (Kaiser & Bengio 2016), ByteNet (Kalchbrenner et al. 2017), and ConvS2S (Gehring et al. 2017) — all convolutional sequence models that dispense with recurrence. It also compares against attention-augmented RNN baselines from prior WMT submissions (§2, Table 2).
Why did convolutional seq2seq models still fall short?

Convolutional models parallelise well but the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input positions grows with distance — linearly for ConvS2S, logarithmically for ByteNet. Self-attention relates any two positions in a constant number of operations, which the paper argues makes long-range dependencies easier to learn (§4).
Is the Transformer the first architecture to use attention?

No. Attention had been used inside RNN-based encoder-decoders (Bahdanau et al. 2015; Luong et al. 2015) and inside convolutional models (Gehring et al. 2017). What's new in this paper is a model that relies *entirely* on attention — no recurrence, no convolutions — which the abstract states explicitly.
What does the paper mean by 'dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely'?

The Transformer's encoder and decoder are stacks of identical layers where the only two operations are multi-head attention and a position-wise feed-forward network. There are no LSTMs, no GRUs, no 1D convolutions. Every representation is computed as a weighted sum of other representations (§1, §3).
Why is auto-regressive generation still needed in a non-recurrent model?

Auto-regression is a property of the output distribution, not the architecture. The paper still models P(y_1, ..., y_n) as ∏ P(y_t | y_{<t}, x), so at inference time the decoder generates one token at a time. The self-attention machinery just replaces the recurrent state — the decoder mask enforces that y_t only sees y_{<t} (§3.2.3).
How does teacher forcing fit into training the Transformer?

During training the decoder is given the entire shifted target sequence and asked to predict the next token at every position in parallel. The mask on the decoder self-attention prevents position t from seeing positions > t, so this is equivalent to running the auto-regressive loop many times at once. This is exactly teacher forcing, just done in one batched matmul rather than serially (§3.2.3, §5.1).
Why do RNN memory issues get worse for longer sequences?

The hidden state has a fixed size but must summarise the entire history to that point. As sequence length grows, either the state saturates (older information gets overwritten) or gradient flow to distant tokens becomes too weak to train. LSTMs and GRUs mitigate but don't eliminate this. Self-attention bypasses it by keeping *all* previous tokens' representations addressable at every layer (§1, §4).
What is 'factorization tricks' in Kuchaiev & Ginsburg 2017 and why is it cited?

The paper cites factorisation tricks as one of several efforts that had recently improved recurrent language models' training efficiency. It's mentioned in §2 to acknowledge that RNN speedups had continued to progress — the paper argues that even so, sequential computation stays a hard ceiling that only removing recurrence entirely can lift.
Why did prior seq2seq systems still have a bottleneck through the last encoder hidden state?

Even with attention, the *representation* of every source token was the encoder's RNN hidden state at that position, which itself was computed sequentially. So the source-side computation was still O(sequence length) sequential steps. The Transformer removes even that: encoder representations are computed in parallel across positions (§1, §3.1).
What did the authors want to prove empirically?

Two things — first, that a model relying entirely on attention could reach state-of-the-art translation quality on well-studied benchmarks (WMT 2014 EN-DE and EN-FR); second, that it could do so at a fraction of the training compute of the previous best systems (Table 2). Both were achieved.
Was the goal purely translation, or did the paper claim broader applicability?

Translation was the headline task, but §6.3 also shows the Transformer generalises to English constituency parsing, matching or beating strong recurrent baselines on WSJ. The paper's broader claim is that self-attention is a useful general primitive, not a translation-specific trick.
How does the number of operations to relate two positions differ across architectures?

Table 1 gives it explicitly. Self-attention: O(1) per layer. Recurrent: O(n). Convolutional: O(log_k(n)) for a dilated stack or O(n/k) for a plain 1D conv. The self-attention advantage is asymptotic and it holds regardless of the specific distance between the two positions being related.
What is the compute cost of self-attention per layer?

Table 1: O(n² · d) where n is the sequence length and d is the representation dimension. It is quadratic in n — that's the trade the paper is making. For the sequence lengths in the paper's experiments (source/target under a few hundred tokens), n² · d is smaller than the recurrent baseline's n · d² because d = 512 and n is small.
When does self-attention become more expensive than a recurrent layer?

When n > d — that is, when the sequence length exceeds the representation dimension. For the paper's setup with d = 512, that's beyond typical sentence-level translation. The paper briefly mentions a restricted variant that only attends to a window of size r around each position, changing the cost to O(r · n · d), for when sequences are long enough that n² matters (§4).
Was memory usage a concern the paper flagged?

It's implicit rather than explicit. The n² attention matrix has memory O(n²) and gets large fast; the paper's translation setups keep sequences short enough that this is fine. Later work (Longformer, Reformer) took the memory issue up seriously, but in this paper the emphasis is on speed.
Why does the paper care about 'training compute' as a metric?

Because the pre-Transformer state of the art required extremely large training budgets — the paper reports prior systems in the ×10^19–10^20 FLOP range (Table 2). Their base Transformer trained to a comparable BLEU in 3.3 × 10^18 FLOPs, which was roughly an order of magnitude less. The compute reduction was a big part of the paper's impact.
What kind of parallelism does the Transformer unlock?

Both within-example parallelism — all n positions of the sequence are processed simultaneously in one matmul — and cross-example batching, which is unchanged. Recurrent models only had cross-example parallelism; the Transformer adds a full sequence-axis parallelism, which is what enabled the 12-hour training runs the paper describes.
Is 'attention is all you need' literally true — could you strip everything else?

The title is deliberately provocative. The Transformer *does* still need feed-forward networks between attention layers, positional encodings, layer normalisation, and residual connections. What it doesn't need is recurrence or convolution as its sequence-mixing primitive. Attention is the sequence primitive; the FFN is the per-position primitive.
What kind of tasks would still favour recurrence?

The paper doesn't make strong negative claims, but tasks with unbounded state — an environment or streaming input the model must summarise over indefinitely — arguably still favour recurrence over full-attention over history. Attention needs the whole history in memory each step.
How does the paper's approach relate to memory networks?

Memory networks and end-to-end memory networks were early examples of attention over an external store. Self-attention is that idea generalised: every token position is a 'memory slot' and every other token attends to it. §2 nods at end-to-end memory networks as prior art in that direction.
Why does §2 emphasise 'constant number of operations'?

Because that's the property that makes gradient flow between distant positions healthy. Constant hop count = no accumulated squashing through many layers of nonlinearity or recurrence, so distant tokens can meaningfully influence each other's representations at every layer of the network (§4).
Does the paper claim self-attention generalises better than recurrence?

It doesn't claim theoretical generalisation guarantees, but §4 does argue self-attention may be easier to interpret because attention distributions can be inspected. It shows some heads attend in ways aligned with syntactic or coreference structure (Figs. 3–5).
What was the state of the art before this paper?

For WMT 2014 EN-DE, the best system was Wu et al.'s Google Neural Machine Translation with model-averaging + ensembling; on EN-FR the best was a deep RNN encoder-decoder ensemble. The base Transformer surpassed all of them, and the big Transformer set new records on both language pairs (Table 2).
Why was translation the chosen benchmark?

Because it was the sequence-to-sequence task with the deepest published baselines and cleanest evaluation (BLEU on WMT). It let the paper compare against strong RNN and CNN baselines under a well-defined metric — no ambiguity about whether the new model was actually better.
Was there any use of pre-training in this paper?

No. The models were trained from scratch on the WMT parallel data (~4.5M sentences for EN-DE, ~36M for EN-FR). Pre-training in the BERT/GPT sense arrived after this paper. Every result in Table 2 is a from-scratch training run.
How does the paper's contribution relate to later work like BERT and GPT?

Those later works kept the Transformer *architecture* and changed the *training objective* — masked language modelling for BERT, autoregressive language modelling at scale for GPT. This paper's contribution was the architecture; the pre-training + transfer paradigm was added later.
What does the overall Transformer architecture look like at a high level?

Encoder stack + decoder stack + linear/softmax at the output. The encoder maps a source sequence of symbol representations to a sequence of continuous representations. The decoder takes those and generates the target sequence one symbol at a time, autoregressively. Both stacks are made of N = 6 identical layers in the base model (§3.1).
Why does the paper use N = 6 layers?

N = 6 is what §3.1 uses for both the encoder and decoder of the base model. It was chosen to give enough depth for the model to compose useful transformations without blowing up training time. The 'big' Transformer uses N = 6 as well but with wider layers (Table 3).
What's in one encoder layer?

Two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention block, then a position-wise feed-forward network. Each sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalisation — the paper writes it as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) (§3.1).
What's in one decoder layer?

Three sub-layers: masked multi-head self-attention over the target sequence so far, then multi-head attention where queries come from the decoder but keys/values come from the encoder output, then a position-wise FFN. Each is wrapped in residual + layer normalisation, same as the encoder (§3.1).
What is d_model and why is it fixed across layers?

d_model = 512 in the base model. It's the dimension of every input and output representation across every layer of the encoder and decoder. Keeping it fixed lets the residual connections work — you can add x and Sublayer(x) only if they have the same dimension. The 'big' model bumps it to 1024 (Table 3).
Why are residual connections used around every sub-layer?

They preserve information across depth and give gradients a direct shortcut back to earlier layers, which helps train deep models. They also mean each sub-layer only has to learn a *delta* from the identity, which is a much easier optimisation problem than learning the whole transformation from scratch.
Why layer normalisation instead of batch normalisation?

Layer norm normalises across the feature dimension of a single token's representation, so it's independent of batch composition and sequence length. Batch norm's statistics depend on batch and would be ill-defined for variable-length sequences with padding. Every published transformer since has stuck with layer norm for the same reason.
Where does the output softmax sit?

At the very top of the decoder stack. The decoder produces a d_model-dimensional vector per output position; a shared learned linear projection maps that to |vocab| logits, and softmax turns those into a distribution over the target vocabulary (§3.4).
What does the paper mean by tying the embedding and softmax weights?

The embedding matrix (used to look up token embeddings) and the linear projection before the softmax (used to score every vocabulary token) share weights. §3.4 says this is done to reduce parameter count and to encourage consistent representations between input and output vocabularies.
Are the encoder and decoder embeddings shared with each other too?

Yes — the paper uses a *shared* source + target vocabulary (byte-pair encoding for EN-DE, word-piece for EN-FR) and a single shared embedding matrix, which is also tied to the pre-softmax projection (§5.1). Three uses of the same matrix.
How does the paper scale the embeddings before adding positional encodings?

It multiplies the embeddings by √d_model before adding positional encodings (§3.4). This puts the embedding magnitudes on a similar scale to the sinusoidal positional encodings so neither dominates the other early in training.
How does information flow from encoder to decoder?

Through the encoder-decoder attention sub-layer in every decoder layer. The queries come from the previous decoder sub-layer; the keys and values come from the top of the encoder stack. So each decoder layer attends to the *final* encoder output, not to intermediate encoder layers (§3.2.3).
Do the decoder layers see the raw source, or the encoder's output?

The encoder's output — the outputs of the topmost encoder layer, which is a length-n source_len sequence of d_model-dim vectors. The decoder never sees the raw token IDs of the source; it sees the encoder's contextualised representations of them.
What are the parameters that the base model actually has?

The base model has about 65M parameters (Table 3, 'base' row). The big model has about 213M. Both fit in a single GPU for training in the paper's setup, though the big model needs more memory and a longer schedule.
What is 'position-wise' about the feed-forward network?

Position-wise means the FFN is applied independently to each position's representation, not across positions. Concretely it's a small MLP applied to each of the n vectors in the sequence in parallel, with the same weights at every position (§3.3).
Do the encoder and decoder use the same FFN?

Same *architecture* — a two-layer MLP with ReLU in between, d_model → d_ff → d_model — but different *weights*. Each of the 12 sub-layers in the base model (6 encoder × 2 FFNs? no — 6 encoder × 1 FFN + 6 decoder × 1 FFN = 12) has its own parameters (§3.3).
How does the decoder handle the fact that the future isn't observed at inference time?

During training, the target sequence is available so the decoder is fed the whole shifted target at once, but masked so position t can only attend to positions ≤ t. At inference time the decoder is called autoregressively — you feed it what it has generated so far, get the next token distribution, sample, feed back in. Same architecture, different call pattern (§3.2.3).
What is the 'start of sequence' token in the Transformer?

The paper uses a standard <s> or equivalent begin-of-sequence token as the first input to the decoder at inference. It doesn't invent a new scheme — this is the same trick as any autoregressive language model. Position 0 of the target is the BOS token; position 1 is what the model predicts first.
Are encoder and decoder trained separately at any point?

No — everything is trained end-to-end from a single loss on the target sequence, which is standard next-token cross-entropy summed over target positions. There's no pre-training of the encoder separately.
What loss function is used?

Token-level cross-entropy on the target sequence, with label smoothing ε_ls = 0.1 (§5.4). The label smoothing hurts perplexity slightly but improves BLEU — the paper flags this as a deliberate trade because the model becomes more uncertain, which is the right calibration for translation.
Why does the decoder use two attention sub-layers instead of one?

The first is *self*-attention over the target sequence so far — the decoder attending to its own previous outputs. The second is *cross*-attention where queries come from the decoder but keys and values come from the encoder — the decoder attending to the source. Separating them lets each sub-layer specialise (§3.1, §3.2.3).
What is the ordering of sub-layers within a decoder layer?

In Figure 1 and §3.1: masked self-attention first, then encoder-decoder attention, then position-wise FFN. Each is wrapped in a residual + LayerNorm. The order matters for interpretability — self-attention integrates target history, cross-attention integrates source, FFN transforms per position.
Where does dropout appear in the architecture?

§5.4 places dropout in three spots: on the output of each sub-layer *before* the residual add + LayerNorm, and on the sum of embeddings + positional encodings at the bottom of the encoder and decoder stacks. Rate P_drop = 0.1 for the base model.
What's the deepest gradient path in the network?

From the loss at position n back to the embedding of position 1, gradients flow through the output softmax, the top decoder layer, then N decoder layers of residual + attention + FFN, into the cross-attention that reaches into the encoder, up through N encoder layers, and back to the embedding. The residuals keep this healthy despite the depth.
What is the attention function the paper defines?

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √d_k) V (§3.2.1, Eq. 1). Queries, keys, and values are matrices; the softmax runs over the last axis; the result is a weighted sum of values where the weights are similarities between queries and keys.
What is d_k and where does it come from?

d_k is the dimension of the key (and query) vectors. In multi-head attention with h = 8 heads and d_model = 512, d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64. It appears in the scaling factor 1/√d_k in the attention formula (§3.2.2).
Why divide by √d_k?

For large d_k, the dot product of two random unit vectors grows in magnitude as √d_k. Feed those into softmax and you get an extremely peaked distribution — near one-hot, near zero gradient for the losing keys. Dividing by √d_k undoes that magnitude growth and keeps the softmax in a regime where gradients are healthy (§3.2.1).
Why not scale by 1/d_k or 1/d_k^2?

Because the variance of the dot product Σ q_i k_i grows *linearly* in d_k when q and k have unit-variance components — its standard deviation grows as √d_k. Dividing by √d_k gives you a dot product with roughly constant variance regardless of d_k, which is what the softmax wants (§3.2.1 footnote 4).
How is attention different from additive attention?

Additive attention (Bahdanau 2015) uses a one-hidden-layer MLP to score query-key pairs: score(q, k) = v^T tanh(W_q q + W_k k). Dot-product attention just uses q^T k. They have similar expressive power, but dot-product is much faster in practice because it becomes a batched matmul (§3.2.1).
So why did people ever use additive attention?

Historically, additive attention was slightly more numerically stable for large d_k because it didn't blow up. Once you add the 1/√d_k scaling to dot-product attention, it matches quality at higher speed — that's what the paper argues. Since then dot-product has dominated.
What are the query, key, and value roles conceptually?

Queries ask 'what am I looking for?' Keys advertise 'what I have to offer for lookup.' Values are 'what I hand back when picked.' The dot product q^T k scores compatibility; softmax turns scores into a distribution; the result is a weighted mixture of values. It's a differentiable soft key-value lookup (§3.2).
Are queries, keys, and values the same vectors or different projections?

Different projections. In self-attention, each token's d_model-dimensional representation gets multiplied by three different learned matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V to produce its query, key, and value vectors of size d_k, d_k, d_v respectively (§3.2.2). Same input, three learned roles.
What is the output shape of one head of attention?

For input queries of shape (n, d_k), keys (m, d_k), values (m, d_v), attention returns (n, d_v). In self-attention over a single sequence, n = m. In cross-attention, n is the target length and m is the source length. Each output row is a d_v-dim value-mixture (§3.2.1).
What if two positions have identical keys?

Then any query aimed at that key direction gets an equal split between them in the softmax and returns a 50/50 mix of their values. There's nothing wrong with that — it's just the model saying 'these two positions look the same to me for this query.'
How does the attention mask work?

The mask sets logits to −∞ (or a very large negative value) at forbidden positions *before* the softmax. Softmax then assigns them zero weight, so the value mixture excludes them. In the decoder self-attention this is used to enforce causality; in encoder self-attention it's used to hide padding tokens (§3.2.3).
Why does the paper use −∞ for masking rather than post-softmax zeroing?

Because zeroing after softmax would break the constraint that attention weights sum to 1 — the remaining weights would still sum to less than one, biasing the output. Masking with −∞ before softmax keeps the surviving weights properly renormalised to sum to 1.
How does gradient flow through the softmax?

Standard softmax Jacobian — each output p_i has ∂p_i/∂z_j = p_i(δ_ij − p_j). Nothing special. The interesting bit is that gradient flows *back through the value mixture* to the values themselves, and *back through the softmax weights* to the queries and keys. Attention is fully differentiable.
Is attention symmetric in the queries and keys?

No — because Q and K are computed by different projections and the softmax runs along a specific axis. Position i attending to position j is not the same operation as j attending to i. In self-attention this asymmetry matters: encoder self-attention has a symmetric attend-anywhere pattern, but decoder self-attention is one-sided by the mask.
What is the computational cost of one attention operation?

Two matmuls dominate: QK^T is O(n · m · d_k) and (softmax(...)) V is O(n · m · d_v). For self-attention n = m so it's O(n² · d). The softmax itself is O(n · m). The paper's Table 1 gives complexity per layer as O(n² · d).
How does attention differ from a convolution?

A 1D convolution mixes only positions within a window of size k around each output position. Attention mixes across every position, weighted by learned similarities — so the receptive field is the whole sequence in one hop, and the weights are content-dependent, not fixed by the layer's parameters.
Is the value dimension d_v allowed to differ from d_k?

Yes, in principle. In practice the paper sets d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64 in every experiment, so keys, queries, and values all share the same head dimension. Nothing in Eq. 1 requires it — only the output projection at the end assumes it.
What happens if you skip the scaling and just use QK^T?

For small d_k it barely matters; for large d_k the softmax saturates and gradients vanish. §3.2.1's footnote is the paper's derivation of why √d_k is the right divisor. Skipping the scale is one of the classic reasons a self-attention implementation looks fine on toy data and fails at scale.
Can attention give a probabilistic interpretation to the value output?

The output is not a probability distribution over values — it's a weighted average. The attention *weights* are a probability distribution over positions. That distinction matters when you want to reason about entropy or uncertainty of the attention itself.
How is attention parallelised across sequence positions?

Every query, key, and value is computed by an independent linear projection per position, which is one big batched matmul. Then Q K^T is a single (n × d_k) × (d_k × n) matmul. Then softmax is elementwise. Then softmax(...) V is another matmul. All n positions computed in one pass — no loop over positions (§3.2).
What is the memory footprint of the attention scores?

O(n²) per attention head — you materialise the full n × n softmax(QK^T / √d_k) matrix. For long sequences this dominates memory. It's the trade the paper is happy to make in a translation setting where n is small; it's what later papers had to address for long-document work.
Can the same attention module be used inside the encoder-decoder attention?

Yes — that's the point. The paper defines one attention module and reuses it in three places: encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention (with a mask), and encoder-decoder attention (where Q comes from the decoder and K, V come from the encoder). Same operation, different inputs (§3.2.3).
Do query and key vectors need to be normalised?

The paper doesn't do explicit normalisation — the scale is handled by the 1/√d_k factor. But you'll see later work (LayerNorm before QKV, or explicit L2 norm on Q and K) that pushes this further to stabilise very deep models. This paper stayed with the simple scaled dot-product.
Is there any temperature parameter on the softmax?

The 1/√d_k factor is effectively a fixed temperature scaling — you can think of it as softmax with temperature √d_k. The paper doesn't make the temperature a separate learnable parameter. If you want to sharpen attention distributions at inference, you can add temperature externally, but training uses the fixed scale.
How would you sanity-check a scaled dot-product implementation?

Give it queries equal to keys and check that the diagonal of QK^T is largest, softmax picks the diagonal, and the output equals the values themselves (identity attention). Any deviation means the scaling or matmul dimensions are wrong. That single check catches most implementation bugs.
What happens if you drop attention weights (like dropout on the softmax output)?

Attention dropout — dropping some softmax weights and renormalising — is a common regulariser. This paper's §5.4 applies dropout to attention *only* through the general 'output of each sub-layer' rule, not a separate attention-specific dropout. Later transformers add attention dropout as a separate knob.
Is scaled dot-product attention the same as key-value memory retrieval?

It's the soft, differentiable version. Traditional key-value retrieval returns the value with the highest key-query similarity; scaled dot-product attention returns a softmax-weighted mixture of values across all keys. The softmax gives you gradients everywhere; the sharpening comes from the network learning to concentrate the softmax.
How do you extend attention to cases where keys and queries live in different spaces?

You keep the projection matrices W_Q, W_K different and let them map into a shared d_k dimension. That's exactly what cross-attention does — queries come from the decoder projection, keys from the encoder projection, and they share a d_k so the dot product is defined (§3.2.3).
What's the role of the value dimension d_v after softmax?

d_v is the dimension of the pre-projection output of the attention head. After all heads run in parallel, their d_v-dim outputs are concatenated to h · d_v = d_model dims and passed through a final linear projection W_O (§3.2.2). d_v controls the per-head expressive capacity of the value mixture.
Does the paper compare against additive attention empirically?

It doesn't include a head-to-head table in the base experiments, but §3.2.1 states that dot-product attention with scaling matches or beats additive attention while being faster because it maps to matmuls. That claim is one of the pragmatic reasons dot-product became the default afterwards.
What is multi-head attention?

Instead of one attention operation with d_model-dimensional Q/K/V, you run h attention operations in parallel — each with its own W_Q^i, W_K^i, W_V^i projecting to d_k = d_model/h dimensions — then concatenate the h outputs and project back with W_O. h = 8 in the base model (§3.2.2).
Why use multiple heads instead of one big head?

Because each head can attend to a different sort of relationship — one head to syntactic dependencies, another to coreference, another to positional structure. §3.2.2 argues that averaging inside a single head would blur these; splitting into heads gives the model multiple 'attention subspaces' to specialise in.
Are the heads doing genuinely different things?

Yes, empirically — Figures 3, 4, and 5 visualise attention heads that align with syntactic head-dependent structure, anaphora resolution, and various positional patterns. The paper's claim isn't that every head is interpretable but that heads specialise enough to be useful in aggregate.
What is the computational cost of multi-head vs. single-head?

Roughly the same. h heads at d_k = d_model/h each cost O(h · n² · d_k) = O(n² · d_model), the same as one big head at d_k = d_model. §3.2.2 makes this trade explicit: multi-head is 'similar in total computational cost.'
Why h = 8?

It was chosen as a good split of d_model = 512 into d_k = 64 subspaces. §5.3's ablation table (Table 3) shows h = 1 hurts quality, h = 4 or 16 are close to h = 8 but not better. The paper landed on 8 as a stable default.
What's the shape of the projection matrices in multi-head attention?

W_Q^i ∈ R^{d_model × d_k}, W_K^i ∈ R^{d_model × d_k}, W_V^i ∈ R^{d_model × d_v} for each head i. W_O ∈ R^{h·d_v × d_model} at the end. Total parameters: 4 · d_model² per multi-head attention block, since h · d_k = h · d_v = d_model (§3.2.2).
How does the concatenation work?

Each head produces an (n × d_v) output. The h outputs are concatenated along the feature axis into a single (n × h·d_v) matrix, then multiplied by W_O to project back to (n × d_model). This is Eq. 2 in the paper (§3.2.2).
Are the head projections computed separately or as one big matmul?

In practice, one big matmul: you stack W_Q^1 ... W_Q^h into a single W_Q ∈ R^{d_model × d_model}, compute Q = XW_Q, then *reshape* the last axis into (h, d_k). The h attentions then run in parallel as a batched matmul. Same math, better GPU utilisation.
What if you set h = 1?
You get single-head attention with d_k = d_model = 512. Table 3 shows this is roughly a full BLEU point worse than h = 8 on EN-DE — the specialisation across heads matters.
What if you set h = 32?

Table 3 shows h = 32 is slightly worse than h = 8. Each head becomes too narrow (d_k = 16), so individual heads can't carry enough signal. The paper's summary is that h somewhere in {4, 8, 16} works; extremes hurt.
Does W_O do anything nontrivial or is it just a shape fix?

It's a learned linear mix across heads. Without W_O you'd have concat(h heads) as your output — but different heads may want to be *combined* rather than just placed side by side. W_O learns that mixture across attention subspaces.
Is multi-head attention different in the encoder vs. the decoder?

The operation is the same; only the inputs differ. Encoder self-attention: Q, K, V all from the same encoder-layer input. Decoder self-attention: Q, K, V from the decoder, plus the causal mask. Encoder-decoder attention: Q from the decoder, K, V from the encoder output (§3.2.3).
What does the paper mean by 'attention head specialization'?

That heads learn different attention patterns. Some heads track syntactic head-modifier links; some resolve pronoun coreference; some just do positional smoothing. Figs. 3–5 show representative examples. It's an emergent property, not an architectural constraint.
Can heads share information during training?

Only through the residual stream — their outputs are combined via W_O and added to the input, so information from all heads is available in the next layer. Within a layer, heads run independently. This is another reason multi-head works: heads can specialise without interfering, and integration happens in the residual + FFN downstream.
Why is dropout not applied inside the multi-head attention block explicitly in the paper?

The paper's §5.4 dropout scheme applies to the output of each sub-layer before the residual add. Multi-head attention as a whole *is* one sub-layer, so its output is dropout'd once, not once per head. Later transformer implementations often add attention dropout (on softmax weights) as an additional knob, but the original paper doesn't.
Does multi-head attention have a limit on how many heads can be useful?

Practically yes — Table 3 shows quality peaks around h = 8. Beyond that, each head becomes too small to carry useful signal. The optimal count is dataset- and task-dependent, but for translation-scale sequences and d_model = 512, h = 8 has been a durable default across many follow-on papers.
What is the total number of parameters in one multi-head attention block?

4 · d_model² = 4 · 512² ≈ 1M parameters for the base model. That's W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O each at d_model × d_model. Times 6 layers × 2 attention blocks per decoder layer (self + cross) = 12 blocks per model side. So multi-head attention accounts for a significant chunk of the base model's ~65M parameters.
Why doesn't the paper make d_k, d_v head-specific?

It could — nothing in the math requires uniform head dimensions. Making them uniform is a simplification that lets you do the entire multi-head operation as one reshape + batched matmul. It's a pragmatic choice, not a theoretical necessity.
How would you inspect what a head is doing after training?

Extract the attention weight matrix for a chosen head at a chosen layer, feed a specific input, and look at the softmax distribution. Figs. 3–5 do this: they show which source tokens each target token attends to for representative heads. It's a straightforward interpretability handle attention gives you that RNNs don't.
Is the paper's h = 8 the same across every layer?
Yes. Every attention block in every layer of both stacks has the same h and same d_k in the base model. Different layers *learn* different head specialisations, but the architectural knob is uniform.
In how many distinct ways is attention used in the Transformer?

Three, per §3.2.3: (1) encoder-decoder attention, where the decoder queries the encoder's outputs; (2) encoder self-attention, where every source position attends to every other source position; (3) decoder self-attention, where every target position attends to earlier target positions (with a causal mask).
What does encoder self-attention accomplish?

It lets every source position see every other source position in one hop, so a token's representation can be built from context anywhere in the source. This replaces the recurrent scan an RNN encoder would do. Because no mask is applied here, information flows in both directions along the source.
Why does decoder self-attention need masking?

To keep training consistent with the auto-regressive inference constraint that position t can only depend on positions < t. Without the mask, the decoder would peek at future target tokens during training and score high — but at inference those future tokens don't exist yet, and the model would fall apart (§3.2.3).
How is the mask implemented?

As an additive matrix M where M[i, j] = 0 if j ≤ i and M[i, j] = −∞ (or a large negative value) if j > i. It's added to the attention scores QK^T / √d_k before softmax. Softmax(−∞) = 0, so those positions get zero attention weight (§3.2.3).
What does encoder-decoder attention accomplish?

It's the mechanism by which the decoder retrieves source information as it generates. Queries come from the decoder (what am I currently trying to translate?), keys and values come from the encoder (what does each source position offer?). This is the closest analogue to the classical attention in RNN seq2seq (§3.2.3).
Do all decoder layers do encoder-decoder attention to the *top* encoder layer?

Yes. §3.2.3: the keys and values come from 'the output of the encoder' — meaning the top encoder layer. Every decoder layer does encoder-decoder attention against the same set of encoder-final representations. Intermediate encoder layers are not exposed to the decoder.
What's the tensor-shape difference between encoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention?

Encoder self-attention: Q, K, V are all (n_src × d_model). Encoder-decoder attention: Q is (n_tgt × d_model), K and V are (n_src × d_model). The resulting attention matrix is (n_tgt × n_src) instead of (n_src × n_src).
Can you use masking in encoder self-attention?

Yes, for padding. If the batch mixes sequences of different lengths, positions beyond the real sequence length in each row are masked out so they don't contribute to or receive attention. The causal mask specifically is only used in the decoder.
Do the three attention uses share parameters?

No. Each of the three uses in each layer has its own W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O. They're all *multi-head attention* modules structurally, but they're separately parameterised. Total attention modules in the model: N encoder × 1 self + N decoder × (1 self + 1 cross) = 6 + 12 = 18 for base.
How does encoder-decoder attention differ from cross-attention in later papers?
It doesn't — 'encoder-decoder attention' is what this paper calls what later work calls 'cross-attention.' Same operation. The paper uses the more descriptive name; later usage shortened it.
Is there attention *within* the FFN?

No. The FFN is a pure per-position MLP — no attention, no mixing across positions. Attention and FFN alternate: attention mixes across positions, FFN transforms within each position. That decomposition is one of the paper's cleanest architectural ideas.
What is the position-wise feed-forward network?

A two-layer MLP applied independently to every sequence position, with the same weights across positions. FFN(x) = max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2 (Eq. 2 in §3.3). W_1 ∈ R^{d_model × d_ff}, W_2 ∈ R^{d_ff × d_model}, with ReLU in between.
What are the dimensions of the FFN in the base model?
d_model = 512 → d_ff = 2048 → d_model = 512. So it widens 4× in the middle, applies ReLU, then narrows back. Table 3 shows d_ff = 2048 for base and 4096 for big.
Why is d_ff four times d_model?

The 4× ratio was picked empirically as a compromise between capacity and cost. Table 3 doesn't ablate d_ff heavily. Later work has stuck with the 4× ratio across many transformer variants, suggesting it's a robust default.
Why 'position-wise'?

Because the FFN is the same 2-layer MLP applied to each of the n positions in parallel, with no mixing across positions. Position-wise means position-independent-of-position. All the cross-position mixing happens in attention; FFN is per-position.
What role does the FFN play in the Transformer's expressive power?

Attention rearranges representations across positions but doesn't add per-position nonlinear transformation capacity. The FFN's ReLU + two linears do that — it can, at each position, compute nonlinear features of the current representation. Without FFN, the model would be limited to linear mixtures across positions.
Are the two FFN layers 'wide-then-narrow' or 'narrow-then-wide'?

Wide-then-narrow. The first layer widens from d_model to d_ff = 4 · d_model, applies ReLU, then the second layer narrows back to d_model. This 'bottleneck' pattern is standard for MLP blocks — you widen so the nonlinearity has room to compute, then narrow so the residual add is dimension-compatible.
Are the FFN weights shared across layers?

No — each of the N encoder layers has its own FFN weights, and each of the N decoder layers has its own too. So the base model has 12 distinct FFN weight sets, each with (d_model × d_ff + d_ff × d_model) = ~2M params, adding up to ~24M params of FFN alone.
Is ReLU the only activation the paper tries?

Yes — ReLU is used throughout (§3.3). The paper doesn't ablate other activations. Later work (Noam Shazeer's GLU variants, GELU in BERT) has shown alternatives can help, but this paper stayed with ReLU.
Why does the Transformer need positional encodings?

Because self-attention is permutation-equivariant. If you shuffle the input positions, the attention output shuffles the same way — the model has no way to distinguish position 1 from position 100. Positional encodings inject that information into the input embeddings (§3.5).
What is the sinusoidal positional encoding formula?

PE(pos, 2i)   = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d_model})
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d_model})
for position pos and dimension i (§3.5, Eq. 3–4). Even-indexed dimensions get sines, odd-indexed get cosines.
Why use sinusoids rather than learned position embeddings?

§3.5 experiments with both and finds nearly identical results (Table 3 row (E)). Sinusoids have one theoretical advantage — the paper argues the model can attend by relative positions because sin(pos+k) is a linear combination of sin(pos) and cos(pos), which the model might exploit to generalise to longer sequences than seen in training.
Do the results actually show sinusoidal beats learned?
No, they're tied on the in-distribution test set. The paper prefers sinusoidal because of the extrapolation-to-longer-sequences argument, not because of a measured quality difference (§3.5).
How are the positional encodings combined with the token embeddings?

By addition. The token embedding at position pos is scaled by √d_model and added to PE(pos) — the result is the input to the first encoder or decoder layer. Same operation for every position (§3.4, §3.5).
What is the wavelength range covered by the sinusoids?

The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π across the d_model dimensions (§3.5). Low dimensions oscillate very fast; high dimensions oscillate very slowly — so together they encode positional information at many different scales.
Do positional encodings limit the maximum sequence length?

Sinusoidal encodings don't — the formula is defined for any positive integer position, so you can compute PE at test time for a longer sequence than at training time. Learned positional embeddings would be limited to the maximum position seen during training. §3.5 flags this as an argument for sinusoids.
Are positional encodings shared between the encoder and the decoder?

Yes, the same formula is used. Each stack's inputs (source embeddings for the encoder, target embeddings for the decoder) get positional encodings added independently, but the formula and the wavelengths are identical (§3.5).
What if positional encodings dominated the token embeddings?

You'd lose token identity. §3.4 multiplies the token embeddings by √d_model precisely to keep them on the same scale as the sinusoidal PE, which has values in [−1, 1]. This scaling matters for stability.
Can the model use positional info in every layer or only the first?

Positional info is added only to the input. But because residual connections preserve information across layers, positional signals propagate all the way to the top of the stack — every layer can 'see' position through the residuals plus what it learned to encode from earlier layers.
Do positional encodings interact with attention masking?

They don't need to. Masking hides certain positions from being attended to; positional encoding tells the model *which* position each token is at. The two work on different axes of the attention computation, so they compose cleanly.
Do the two neighbouring sinusoid pairs (sin, cos) at dimension i encode the same information?

They encode complementary phase — sin and cos at the same wavelength let you reconstruct position modulo that wavelength unambiguously. Together, the full set of (sin, cos) pairs across all wavelengths gives a unique fingerprint for each position within the modelled range.
What three desiderata does §4 use to compare architectures?

Total computational complexity per layer, amount of computation that can be parallelised (measured as minimum sequential operations required), and maximum path length between long-range dependencies. Table 1 summarises where self-attention, recurrent, and convolutional layers land on each (§4).
What is the 'maximum path length' the paper emphasises?

The maximum number of operations any signal needs to traverse to influence any other position — because gradient signal degrades with path length. Self-attention: O(1). Recurrent: O(n). Convolutional: O(log_k(n)) with dilated convs. Short paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn (§4).
Why does §4 say self-attention could produce more interpretable models?

Because you can visualise the attention weights and inspect which positions each output attends to. §4 shows this in Figs. 3–5 — heads that seem to track syntactic dependencies, coreference, and other linguistic phenomena. Not a proof of interpretability, but a concrete affordance RNNs don't have.
What is the restricted self-attention variant §4 mentions?

A version that only attends to a window of size r around each position, giving cost O(r · n · d) and maximum path length O(n/r). It's a knob for when n² is too big — you trade some receptive-field width for compute. The paper doesn't use it in the main experiments but flags it for longer sequences (§4).
Does self-attention have any drawbacks compared to CNNs or RNNs?

The n² memory cost is the big one — it dominates for long sequences and doesn't fit in accelerator memory for very long documents. RNNs have O(n) memory. CNNs are between the two. This paper's translation setup keeps n small enough that self-attention's cost is acceptable, but it's not always.
How does the paper's argument in §4 relate to the empirical BLEU results?

Loosely — the argument is that self-attention should be easier to optimise for long-range dependencies, which should show up as better translation quality. Table 2 confirms improved BLEU. §4 doesn't prove causation, just plausibility, and the empirical section carries the actual weight.
Is a stack of self-attention layers strictly more expressive than a stack of recurrent layers?

The paper doesn't make a formal expressivity claim. Both are universal approximators in appropriate limits. The paper's argument is about *trainability* — self-attention's constant path length and parallelism make it easier to train in practice, especially for long-range dependencies.
What dataset did the paper train on for EN-DE?

WMT 2014 English-to-German, about 4.5M sentence pairs. Encoded with a shared byte-pair encoding vocabulary of ~37,000 tokens. Newstest2013 was used as the development set; newstest2014 for the reported BLEU (§5.1).
What about EN-FR?
WMT 2014 English-to-French, ~36M sentence pairs, ~32,000 word-piece vocabulary. Same evaluation protocol — newstest2013 dev, newstest2014 test (§5.1).
How were sentences batched during training?

Each training batch contained sentences of similar length, up to about 25,000 source tokens and 25,000 target tokens (§5.1). Batching by length reduces wasted computation on padding — sentences of similar length pad less.
What hardware was training done on?
8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs (§5.2). The base model trained for 100,000 steps at ~0.4s per step, about 12 hours total. The big model trained for 300,000 steps at ~1s per step, about 3.5 days total.
What optimiser is used?

Adam with β_1 = 0.9, β_2 = 0.98, ε = 10^{-9} (§5.3). Note the unusually low β_2 = 0.98 — not the default 0.999. This gives the second-moment estimate a shorter effective time window, which seemed to help stability.
What is the learning-rate schedule?

lrate = d_model^{−0.5} · min(step^{−0.5}, step · warmup^{−1.5}), with warmup = 4000 steps (Eq. 3, §5.3). Linear warm-up from zero for the first 4000 steps, then inverse-square-root decay. This is now called 'Noam schedule' after the second author.
Why warm up the learning rate at all?

Because Adam's second-moment estimator is very noisy at the start of training — a full learning rate early can push weights in bad directions before the moments are stable. Linear warmup lets the moments settle in before you take big steps.
Why inverse-square-root decay rather than exponential or step decay?

It's smoother and it matches the theoretical Adam convergence rate more closely. It also has one hyperparameter — the warmup length — instead of several. The paper doesn't claim theoretical optimality, but it's a robust default that many follow-on papers adopted.
What was the base model's total training time?
About 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs, or roughly 3.3 × 10^18 FLOPs total (Table 2). The paper contrasts this with prior best systems' 10^19–10^20 FLOPs training budgets.
What was the big model's total training time?
About 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs, or roughly 2.3 × 10^19 FLOPs total (Table 2). Still comparable to or below prior best systems while achieving new SOTA on EN-DE and EN-FR.
How were checkpoints averaged?

For the base model, the last 5 checkpoints (saved at 10-minute intervals) were averaged. For the big model, the last 20 checkpoints (§5.4, end). Checkpoint averaging is a simple ensemble-of-the-past technique that consistently helped.
What is the label smoothing rate and why?

ε_ls = 0.1 (§5.4). Instead of assigning probability 1.0 to the target token and 0 elsewhere, you assign (1 − ε_ls) to the target and spread ε_ls over the rest. This penalises overconfidence — perplexity goes up but BLEU also goes up, meaning the model is calibrated better for translation.
Does label smoothing help all metrics?

No — it hurts perplexity slightly. The paper flags this trade explicitly (§5.4): the model becomes less certain per-token but its outputs correlate better with reference translations, so BLEU rises. Which metric matters depends on the downstream use.
What regularisers does the paper use?

Two: residual dropout with P_drop = 0.1, and label smoothing with ε_ls = 0.1. The dropout is applied to the output of each sub-layer before the residual add, and to the sum of embeddings and positional encodings (§5.4).
Why not weight decay?

The paper doesn't mention it explicitly. Adam-style optimisers can interact poorly with weight decay (AdamW came later specifically to address this). Dropout + label smoothing + the natural regularisation from a large-ish dataset were enough.
Where exactly is dropout applied?

§5.4 places it in three spots: on the output of each sub-layer *before* the residual + LayerNorm, on the sum of embeddings and positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder inputs, and (implicitly) on the attention outputs since those pass through the same sub-layer output path.
What dropout rate is used for the big model?

P_drop = 0.3 for EN-DE (§5.4) — noticeably higher than the base model's 0.1. The bigger model has more parameters and needs more regularisation to avoid overfitting on the same-sized dataset. EN-FR big uses P_drop = 0.1 because its dataset is much bigger.
Does dropout during training slow inference at all?

No — dropout is turned off at inference time. All weights are used deterministically. The model is trained with dropout so that no single unit becomes indispensable, but at test time you get the full network's response.
Is there any noise on the input?
Not explicitly. No input dropout, no denoising, no data augmentation on the raw text. The regularisation is entirely at the model level — sub-layer dropout + label smoothing.
What is the reported BLEU score on WMT 2014 English-to-German?

28.4 for the big Transformer (§5.5, Table 2), which was a new state of the art at the time, over 2 BLEU above the previous best ensemble. The base Transformer scored 27.3 — also above every previous single model.
What about English-to-French?
41.8 for the big Transformer on WMT 2014 EN-FR (Table 2), also a new SOTA. Base scored 38.1. Both were achieved at a fraction of the previous best systems' training cost.
How much less training compute did the Transformer use versus prior best?
Roughly 10× less for the big model — 2.3 × 10^19 FLOPs versus prior systems' 10^20 FLOPs (Table 2). The base model at 3.3 × 10^18 FLOPs was about 100× cheaper than the previous single-model best.
What did §5.4's ablations vary?

Table 3 varies the number of heads h, the head dimensions d_k and d_v, the model dimension d_model, the FFN width d_ff, the dropout rate, and whether positional encodings are learned or sinusoidal. Each is measured on newstest2013 EN-DE.
What was the biggest quality lever in the ablations?

The number of layers N and the number of attention heads h had the largest effects. Reducing N to 2 lost about 4 BLEU. h = 1 lost about 1 BLEU. Model dimension and dropout also mattered but less dramatically (Table 3).
What did the ablation on positional encoding show?

Learned vs sinusoidal was essentially tied on newstest2013 EN-DE — the paper (row E of Table 3) reports 25.7 vs 25.8 BLEU. The choice was pragmatic: sinusoidal has the extrapolation-to-longer-sequences property, learned doesn't.
Did the paper try English constituency parsing?

Yes, §6.3. Trained on the WSJ portion of the Penn Treebank (40K sentences) or in a semi-supervised setting with the BerkeleyParser corpora. The Transformer matched or beat strong RNN-based baselines, showing the architecture generalised beyond translation.
What was the parsing F1 score?

91.3 F1 in the WSJ-only setting and 92.7 F1 in the semi-supervised setting (Table 4). The paper's point is not to set a new parsing record but to show the architecture works out-of-the-box on a different structured-prediction task.
How did the paper handle rare words at inference time?

BPE for EN-DE and word-piece for EN-FR are subword vocabularies, so out-of-vocabulary words are automatically split into learned subwords. This is standard practice — the paper didn't invent anything special for rare-word handling (§5.1).
What decoding scheme is used at inference time?

Beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty α = 0.6 (§6.1). Also, max output length was set to input length + 50 to avoid runaway generation. Standard seq2seq decoding — the model architecture is what changed, not the search.
Did the paper release code or checkpoints?

Yes — a reference implementation was published in the Tensor2Tensor library at the same time as the paper. That code became the basis for many follow-on transformer implementations. The paper cites it explicitly.
Are the numbers reproducible?

Broadly yes — the Tensor2Tensor implementation lets you re-run WMT 2014 EN-DE with the paper's hyperparameters and get within noise of the reported BLEU. Small variations come from data preprocessing choices and hardware differences, not from the model itself.
How did the ablation on d_k change performance?

Row (B) of Table 3: reducing d_k without changing anything else hurt quality — smaller keys mean less discriminative attention scoring, and the model can't attend precisely. This aligned with the theoretical concern about scaled dot-product's variance.
Did the paper try training much longer?

The base model was trained for 100K steps, the big model for 300K. Both are well past the point where BLEU plateaued. Longer schedules were not the constraint — the paper's point was that the Transformer *converges fast*, not that longer is always better.
Did the paper explore ensembling?

Only lightly — checkpoint averaging over the last 5 or 20 checkpoints is a form of self-ensemble. Full model ensembles across independent training runs weren't the focus. The reported single-model numbers are what's compared in Table 2.
If I were implementing this today, what's the first thing I should get right?

The masking — both the causal mask in the decoder self-attention and the padding mask in the encoder self-attention. Silent masking bugs are the most common Transformer bug. Add a unit test: feed dummy inputs and check that softmax weights on masked positions are exactly zero.
Should I use pre-norm or post-norm?

The paper uses post-norm: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). Pre-norm — LayerNorm before the sub-layer, add residual outside — was introduced later to make very deep transformers train more stably. For this paper's depth (N = 6), post-norm works. For depth 24+, most modern implementations prefer pre-norm.
How do I set d_model and d_ff for my own dataset?

The paper's ratios — d_ff = 4 · d_model, d_k = d_model / h — are robust starting points. Pick d_model based on how much compute you have (bigger is better up to a point) and how many parameters you can afford. Everything else follows.
What's the smallest useful Transformer configuration?

N = 4 or 6 layers, d_model = 256 or 512, h = 4 or 8, d_ff = 1024 or 2048 — you can train that on a single GPU on a modest dataset. The paper's base config is a good starting point; halving each dimension is a reasonable smaller variant.
How do I know if my attention is actually attending to something?

Save a few attention weight matrices from a trained model. If they're near-uniform across positions, the model isn't using attention meaningfully. If they concentrate on specific position patterns — diagonal, local windows, syntactic-looking — attention is working. This is the diagnostic Figs. 3–5 in the paper demonstrate.
What happens if I forget the positional encodings?

The model becomes permutation-invariant to the input. It would train, but it would learn bag-of-tokens representations, not sequence models. On translation you'd see BLEU stall near random. This is the second most common Transformer bug after masking.
How do I diagnose an exploding loss during Transformer training?

Two usual suspects. First, learning rate too high without warmup — the paper's 4000-step warmup exists precisely because Adam's second moments are unstable early. Second, missing the 1/√d_k scaling — makes softmax saturate and gradients explode. Check both.
What's the biggest single lever for translation quality in the paper's setup?

Model size — moving from base (65M params) to big (213M) picks up over a BLEU point on both EN-DE and EN-FR. That was the paper's clearest empirical trend and one of the seeds of the scaling laws work that came later.
Should I always use label smoothing?

For any task where output calibration matters and you evaluate with a metric that rewards diverse plausible outputs (BLEU, ROUGE), yes. For tasks where sharp per-token predictions matter more (classification, exact-match extraction), it's less clearly beneficial. This paper's translation task is a textbook fit.
How do I extend this to a longer input than the paper handles?

Three options. Sparse attention (windowed or strided) reduces the n² cost. Linformer / Performer / other kernel approximations replace the softmax with cheaper alternatives. Or chunk the input and process chunks separately. This paper doesn't cover any of these — long-context transformer research became its own subfield afterwards.
Do I need to warm up the learning rate on modern hardware?

Yes — the reason (Adam's second-moment instability early in training) is architectural, not hardware-dependent. Modern transformer training universally uses some form of warmup. The specific 4000-step Noam schedule is a starting point; you can adjust warmup length based on your dataset size and batch size.
How do I choose between sinusoidal and learned positional encodings?

If you'll evaluate on sequences longer than the training set, use sinusoidal — you get the extrapolation for free. If your inference sequences are bounded by your training-set max length, learned embeddings work fine. This paper's Table 3 shows the quality difference is small either way.
What is the effect of batch size on Transformer training?

Bigger batches let the optimiser see better gradient estimates per step and reduce total wall-clock time. The paper's 25,000-source-token batches are on the large side by 2017 standards. Modern training routinely uses batches of hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens, distributed across many GPUs.
Can the same architecture be used for autoregressive language modelling?

Yes — that's what GPT does. Take the decoder half of the Transformer, remove the cross-attention sub-layer (there's no encoder), and train it on next-token prediction. The architecture in this paper is the direct parent of both GPT (decoder-only) and BERT (encoder-only).
Can I encode multiple modalities into the same Transformer?

Yes, with modality-specific tokenisation. Vision transformers do this by tokenising image patches. Audio transformers tokenise spectrogram frames. The core architecture — attention over a sequence of embeddings + FFN + residuals — is modality-agnostic; only the tokeniser is modality-specific.
How does this paper relate to Universal Transformers / Adaptive Computation Time?

It predates them. This paper uses a fixed N = 6 layers. Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al. 2018) tie weights across layers and apply Adaptive Computation Time to pick layer count per token. That's a follow-on line of work; this paper stayed with fixed-depth stacks.
Is there anything specific about the paper's Adam ε = 10^{-9}?

It's smaller than PyTorch's default 10^{-8} but doesn't change training behaviour meaningfully. The paper likely used TensorFlow's default at the time. If you're rewriting the paper's setup today, either ε value is fine.
Should I use the paper's exact hyperparameters as a starting point today?

For translation on WMT-scale data, yes. For other tasks (language modelling, classification, code generation), the *ratios* — d_ff = 4·d_model, d_k = d_model/h, alpha = 2r for LoRA later — are more portable than the absolute numbers. Start with the paper's ratios and scale d_model to your compute budget.
What's the single line of the paper I'd re-read most often?

'The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.' That sentence in the abstract compresses the paper's whole argument into one claim about speed + quality.
What does 'attention is all you need' most concretely mean for a first-time implementer?

That you don't need to build recurrence or convolution to model sequences — you can compose (multi-head attention + FFN + residuals + layer norm + positional encodings) into a stack and it will learn to model sequential structure. The mental model is much smaller than an LSTM's, and the code is much more parallel.
Why does the paper add positional encodings to embeddings rather than concatenate them?

Concatenation would grow d_model by the positional-encoding dimension, changing every downstream weight shape. Addition keeps d_model fixed, which is what the residual connections need. It also mixes positional information into every feature dimension immediately rather than segregating it into its own slice.
What happens to positional encoding through many layers of residuals?

The information persists - every layer's output is x + Sublayer(x), and the positional signal in x flows through the residual to the next layer. The model can also learn to strengthen or weaken the positional signal through the sublayer's transformation. Empirically, positional information stays available all the way to the top.
Can I compute attention over a very long input by chunking?

You can chunk the input, run self-attention within each chunk, and then handle cross-chunk dependencies with a hierarchical or sliding-window scheme. The paper does not do this - its sequences are short enough - but it is a common practical extension for document-length inputs.
What is the intuition for why label smoothing helps BLEU?

Because BLEU rewards diverse n-gram overlap with the reference, and a model that assigns some probability mass to plausible alternatives will decode more varied outputs at test time. Label smoothing prevents the model from spiking probability on the reference token so hard that decoding always picks the highest-probability continuation blindly.
What is the purpose of Adam second-moment beta_2 = 0.98?

Lower beta_2 makes the running average of squared gradients react faster to recent gradients. In the highly non-stationary early phase of Transformer training this helps the optimiser adapt more quickly. The paper picked 0.98 empirically; it is a small but repeatable improvement over the default 0.999.
Why does the Transformer use beam search rather than sampling at test time?

Because translation is evaluated with BLEU, which rewards high-precision output - you want the most likely translation, not a diverse one. Beam search approximates arg-max over the joint distribution; sampling would be preferred for tasks like story generation where diversity matters.
How does the causal mask interact with padding?

You need both. The causal mask hides the future within each sequence; the padding mask hides positions beyond the real length of each sequence in the batch. Combine them into a single additive mask before softmax - union of both sets of minus-infinity positions.
What is the wall-clock difference between attention and recurrent training in practice?

The paper reports 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs for the base Transformer to reach 27.3 BLEU on EN-DE. Comparable RNN systems of the era needed multiple days on similar hardware to reach lower BLEU. The gap is primarily from within-example parallelism, not from any per-step efficiency.
How does the number of parameters in attention compare to the FFN?

Per encoder layer in the base model: attention has 4 * d_model^2 = ~1M parameters (W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O). FFN has 2 * d_model * d_ff = ~2M parameters. So FFN is roughly 2x attention in parameter count. Aggregated across the whole model, FFN accounts for more parameters than attention.
Is the Transformer's performance sensitive to random initialisation?

It is sensitive enough that different seeds give BLEU differences of a few tenths, which is why checkpoint averaging helps. The Xavier-style initialisation and the warmup schedule together keep initial training stable. Very deep transformers need more careful initialisation (Fixup, T-Fixup came later).
Can I skip the positional encodings if my task is unordered?

For genuinely unordered inputs - sets - yes, you can drop positional encodings and use a Transformer as a permutation-invariant set encoder. That is Deep Sets territory. This paper's tasks are ordered, so positional encodings matter.
Does the paper argue for or against dropout on attention weights?

It does not discuss softmax dropout explicitly. Section 5.4's dropout is on sub-layer outputs, not on attention weights specifically. Later transformers often add attention-weight dropout as an additional regulariser, especially for large models trained on modest data.
What if I used a sinusoidal positional encoding with a different base than 10000?

The base 10000 controls the range of wavelengths spanned. Smaller bases compress the range and hurt long-position discrimination; larger bases spread it and can make short-distance discrimination less crisp. The paper landed on 10000 empirically; small variations do not change much.
Why does the paper report BLEU rather than perplexity as the headline metric?

Because perplexity measures how well the model predicts tokens, but BLEU measures translation quality, and those two are correlated only loosely. Label smoothing hurts perplexity but helps BLEU. Translation researchers care about BLEU, so BLEU is what Table 2 tracks.
What is the single most important architectural idea to walk away with?

Attention as a differentiable soft key-value lookup - every position can retrieve context from every other position in one operation, weighted by learned similarity. Everything else in the paper is scaffolding to make that idea work at translation scale: multi-head for specialisation, positional encodings for order, residuals + LayerNorm for depth, FFN for per-position nonlinearity.
